paper_title: A Reinforcement Learning Method to Navigate SMEFT Operator Space

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: In particle physics, discrepancies between experimental measurements and Standard Model (SM) predictions are commonly interpreted within new theoretical models. In this context, the Standard Model Effective Field Theory (SMEFT) provides a general framework encompassing a broad class of models. However, exploring the enormous space of possible SMEFT operators rapidly becomes a challenging combinatorial problem: many operators can contribute simultaneously to different observables, their effects are correlated, and distinct operator combinations can provide comparably good descriptions of the data. In this work, we formulate the exploration of the SMEFT operator space as a sequential decision-making problem using reinforcement learning (RL). Our RL agent employs a lightweight actor-critic architecture with approximately 40K trainable parameters in total. Rather than searching for a single best-fit theory, our method is designed to discover a diverse set of high-quality theory hypotheses. We test the method in a complex phenomenological environment comprising 132 observables across several sectors of particle physics, including 24 measurements that deviate from their SM predictions by more than $1.5σ$. We show that the learned RL policy efficiently constructs multi-operator theories that substantially improve the global fit. Comparisons with independent random-subset and random-sequential searches demonstrate the ability of the RL policy to navigate this large combinatorial space. Our results establish RL as a systematic framework for exploring diverse patterns of new physics (NP) interactions within SMEFT.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: The SM provides successful description of particle physics over wide range of energy scales. Nevertheless, it cannot account for several important observations such as neutrino masses, dark matter, and the baryon asymmetry of the universe. This motivates the presence of physics beyond the SM (BSM). At the same time, direct searches at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) have so far revealed no conclusive evidence for such NP. If the scale of NP lies much above the energies directly accessible to current colliders, its effects may instead first appear indirectly through deviations of low-energy observables from their SM predictions, i.e., anomalies. Effective field theories (EFTs) provide model-independent framework for interpreting such discrepancies. Above the electroweak scale, the effects of heavy NP can be parameterized within the Standard Model Effective Field Theory (SMEFT) Buchmuller and Wyler [1986], Grzadkowski et al. [2010](for the reviews, see Brivio and Trott [2019], Isidori et al. [2024], Aebischer et al. [2026]), 1The implementation of our RL framework and the accompanying analysis tools and data are publicly available as open-source software: ReinforceSMEFT. Preprint. which contains only SM fields and respects the SU (3)C SU (2)L (1)Y gauge symmetry. Below the electroweak scale, the appropriate description is the Weak Effective Theory (WET), obtained after integrating out the heavy SM degrees of freedom and respecting SU (3)C (1)em. Statement of the problem: central problem in indirect searches for NP is the following: given collection of experimental measurements, which combinations of SMEFT operators can improve the agreement with the data while remaining compatible with the other experimental constraints? This bottom-up problem is an important intermediate step toward the eventual top-down question of identifying UV theories capable of generating the preferred SMEFT operators. However, the difficulty arises from the enormous combinatorial space of the SMEFT operators. At dimension six, the Warsaw basis Grzadkowski et al. [2010] contains 59 baryon and lepton number conserving operators, corresponding to 2499 independent operators once flavour indices are taken into account. Even when only subset of these operators is relevant to particular low-energy dataset, the number of possible multi-operator hypotheses grows rapidly. For candidate operators, the number of possible theories containing up to operators is Ncomb = (cid:88) n=1 (cid:19) . (cid:18)N (1) Here is total number of SMEFT operators considered in problem, and represents the number of operators in given SMEFT hypothesis. In the present analysis, we work with 912 SMEFT operators that conserve the baryon number, lepton number, and lepton flavour. The challenge is therefore not simply to determine the continuous values of set of WCs, but first to determine which operators should be present. This introduces discrete combinatorial search problem on top of the usual continuous parameter estimation. Importantly, SMEFT operators cannot generally be considered independent because single operator may affect multiple observables. These correlations become even richer after renormalization-group (RG) evolution and matching between SMEFT and WET Aebischer et al. [2026]. Operator mixing due to RG running implies that an operator introduced to improve one observable may simultaneously modify several others. In order to interpret experimental measurements within SMEFT, therefore it requires understanding of non-trivial correlations among different directions in the operator space. These correlations are particularly important for multi-operator SMEFT hypotheses. An operator that improves the description of one discrepant observable may worsen agreement with another measurement. second operator can then compensate for this deterioration while preserving, or further improving, the original effect. Subsequent operators can similarly repair constraints or address additional discrepancies. Consequently, the quality of multi-operator hypothesis cannot in general be inferred from the performance of its constituent operators in isolation. Viable solutions can instead emerge through correlated combination of operators. Conventional phenomenological analyses address this complexity using physics intuition to restrict the set of operators under consideration, often guided by particular UV theory, symmetry argument, or simplified model. Such approaches are very useful for testing specific hypotheses, but necessarily explore only small fraction of the complete SMEFT operator space. At the opposite extreme, exhaustive enumeration of all possible operator combinations quickly becomes computationally prohibitive. In this work, we formulate the search for viable SMEFT operators sequential decision making problem using an actor-critic" RL algorithm Sutton et al. [1999], Sutton and Barto [2018] as introduced below. Reinforcement learning method: We design an RL policy using transformer Vaswani et al. [2023] based neural-network (NN) which learns to propose viable SMEFT operators combinations through repeated interactions with phenomenological environment. So instead of evaluating every SMEFT operator combination independently, an RL policy can construct multi-operator hypothesis sequentially, observe how the global fit to experimental data changes, and use this feedback to adjusts the NN weights to learn. An important feature of this formulation is that the policy can learn conditional operator preferences. If the addition of one operator repeatedly produces characteristic pattern of improvements and deterioration among observables, the policy can learn which subsequent operators are effective in 2 that particular state. The RL agent 2 therefore does not merely learn global ranking of individual operators, it learns how useful an operator is conditional on the presence of other operators. We stress that our objective is broader than identifying single best-fit theory. Different combinations of SMEFT operators can provide comparably good descriptions of the same data, and identifying this degeneracy is itself important for model building. We therefore formulate the task as quality diversity search: the agent should discover high-quality solutions while continuing to explore structurally different regions of the SMEFT operator space. To achieve this, we supplement the fit-quality reward Kumar et al. [2026] with novelty-based reward function that discourages repeated sampling of closely related operator sets. The details of RL formulation are given in the next section. Related efforts have recently explored the use of machine learning (ML) and artificial intelligence (AI) techniques for automated theory exploration in particle physics. For example, Ref. Baretz et al. [2026] developed the Autonomous Model Builder (AMBer), which employs RL to construct viable neutrino-flavor models by selecting symmetry groups, particle content, and representation assignments. Ref. Alexander et al. [2026] proposed the autonomous discovery of particle physics theories directly from experimental data using RL and symbolic-regression techniques. Ref. Hammad and Sanz [2026] explored complementary language-model-based approach in which domainadapted LLM generates hypotheses for sparse SMEFT analyses, while Ref. Saad [2026] developed an LLM-assisted framework for BSM model building, in which an LLM provides natural-language interface to deterministic symbolic backend that automatically constructs and analyzes BSM models from user-specified field content. These studies illustrate the growing interest in using ML to navigate large theory space and facilitate traditionally human-guided aspects of model building in particle physics. Code availability: The method presented in this work builds upon my open-source GitHub implementation ReinforcePhysics. This RL framework includes implementations based on both the actorcritic" algorithm and Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO)Shao et al. [2024]; in the present work, we focus on the former. To facilitate reproducibility and broader use, we have packaged the complete methodology into the pip-installable Python package, which is publicly available and will be actively maintained in the ReinforceSMEFT GitHub repository.

Starting from the SM, the RL agent proposes one SMEFT operator at each time step t. The Wilson coefficients (WCs) of the currently proposed operators are optimized by minimizing the global χ2, and the resulting improvement in the fit along with diversity criteria provides the primary feedback to the agent in terms of rewards. Initially, proposed operator is temporarily added to the currently accepted operator set and the corresponding χ2 is minimized. The operator is retained if it improves the fit by more than χ2 min = 2 and is rejected otherwise. During training, the policy learns to assign larger probabilities to operator selections that lead to larger cumulative future rewards. Consequently, the agent is not restricted to selecting operators that provide the largest immediate improvement in the fit; it can learn sequences in which an operator produces only modest initial improvement but enables subsequent operators to achieve substantially better global fit. The basic idea of the actorcritic algorithm is straightforward: actor is simply the policy πθ(atst), which we parameterize by small transformerbased NN. It determines the probability of selecting action at (or an SMEFT operator Ot) in given state st. The critic estimates the expected future return from the current state and thereby provides baseline for the policy-gradient update. Here, the return is defined by the cumulative discounted reward obtained from the current state onward when following the current policy πθ. In terms of the so-called true value function" π(st), the advantage is defined as At = Gt π(st). (5) However, since the true value function π(st) is not known, we train separate NN, the critic, to approximate it by Vϕ(st), where ϕ denotes the learnable critic parameters. For each batch of sampled trajectories, the critic is trained using the objective Lcritic(ϕ) = (cid:88) [Vϕ(st) Gt]2 . (6) Here, denotes the total number of sampled stateaction steps entering the corresponding training update. Training proceeds iteratively by sampling batches of trajectories from the current policy πθ and using them to update the network parameters. For the actor, the gradient θLactor increases the probability of actions with positive advantage and suppresses those with negative advantage. Importantly, At is treated as fixed target when computing the actor gradient. sections.title: 3 RL Environment
sections.content: The SMEFT operators are sampled sequentially using the current policy πθ. After each operator is sampled in trajectory, our framework invokes an internal χ2-minimization procedure to evaluate the resulting fit and determine the corresponding reward. Since training the RL policy requires large number of such interactions with the environment, this procedure must be repeated many times. direct evaluation of the χ2 function would require performing the full RG evolution within SMEFT and WET, followed by the computation of the relevant observables, for every proposed set of operators. Combined with the repeated χ2 minimization, this would render the RL training prohibitively expensive. To overcome this computational bottleneck, we precompute semi-analytic expressions for the observables, retaining their linear dependence on the SMEFT WCs defined at the NP scale. The computationally expensive RG evolution and observable calculations are therefore performed only once during this preprocessing stage. The resulting expressions can subsequently be evaluated very efficiently within the RL environment, enabling rapid computation of the χ2 function and the corresponding rewards throughout training. 3.1 Semianalytic χ2 function At dimension-six level in SMEFT, the theoretical prediction for an observable can be written as Oth,a({Ci}) = OSM,a + (cid:88) αaiCi(Λ) + (cid:88) j,k, jk βa,jkCj(Λ)Ck(Λ) (20) where Ci(Λ) are the WCs defined at the NP scale Λ. The coefficients αai and βa,jk encode, respectively, the linear and quadratic dependence of observable on the SMEFT WCs, including the effects of RG evolution and matching at the electroweak scale. We assume CP-conserving SMEFT scenario, such that the WCs are real. In the present analysis, we retain only the linear contribution proportional to αai and construct the corresponding semi-analytic expression for each observable included in the global fit. We emphasize, however, that the RL method itself is not restricted to the linear approximation and can also be applied when quadratic terms are retained. The χ2 function is defined as χ2({Ci}) = (cid:88) [Oth,a({Ci}) Oexp,a]2 σ2 th,a + σ2 exp,a (21) where Oexp,a denotes the experimental measurement, while σth,a and σexp,a denote the corresponding theoretical and experimental uncertainties, respectively. To determine the semi-analytic coefficients, we use flavio Straub [2018] for the computation of observable predictions and wilson Aebischer et al. [2018a] for RG evolution. The computationally expensive SMEFT calculations are therefore performed only once when constructing the semi-analytic expressions, while the subsequent χ2 evaluations required repeatedly during RL training can be carried out efficiently using these precomputed expressions. We find that the RL training would be extremely slow without following this procedure. 7 3.2 Benchmark dataset To test the RL method introduced in this work, we construct sufficiently complex benchmark environment. For this purpose, we consider hypothetical dataset4 consisting of 132 observables drawn from several sectors of particle physics, including electroweak precision observables, Band K-meson processes, τ decays, leptonic magnetic moments, Higgs observables, and scattering measurements. Within SMEFT, these sectors are not independent: correlations arise through gauge symmetry, RG evolution, matching, and dimension-six modifications of SM input parameters Aebischer et al. [2026]. Among the 132 observables in our dataset, 24 differ from their chosen SM predictions by more than 1.5σ, resulting in χ2 SM = 273. These observables are listed in Tab. 1. The remaining measurements act as constraints on the candidate operator sets. The sole purpose of this dataset is to provide challenging benchmark containing complex pattern of discrepancies with respect to the SM for the RL search algorithm. sections.title: 4 Training of the RL Policy
sections.content: The objective of RL training is to learn policy (or policies) through repeated interaction with the environment. The SMEFT operators that produce large improvements in the fit and satisfy the diversity criteria become more likely, whereas choices associated with poor trajectories are suppressed. 4Although real measurements are used for some observables, we refer to the overall dataset as hypothetical because it also contains fictitious measurements. In addition, the real measurements included in the benchmark are not necessarily up to date. The SM predictions and their corresponding uncertainties, on the other hand, are computed using flavio. 8 As an example, for training, we use 300 batches, with 25 stochastic trajectories sampled per batch and at most = 10 proposals per trajectory. Since the RL search is sequential, in total, it involve 300 25 10 = 75K calls to the internal χ2-minimization loop. Without using the pre-computed semi-analytical expressions, it would computationally very expensive. We use MINUIT James and Roos [1975] for the χ2 minimization. The actor and critic are optimized using AdamW with learning rate of 103. We use discount factor γ = 0.99, critic-loss coefficient λV = 0.5, and gradient clipping at 0.5. An entropy term is included during training to prevent premature collapse of the policy and maintain exploration; its coefficient is annealed from 102 to 104. The complete set of training hyperparameters and other details can be found on GitHub ReinforceSMEFT. Fig. 1 shows the evolution of fit quality during training. For each batch, we display the mean and maximum χ2 obtained by the sampled trajectories, together with the best value discovered up to that point. The raw batch values fluctuate substantially because the policy remains stochastic and is explicitly encouraged to explore through both entropy regularization and diversity reward. Consequently, the mean or maximum χ2 of an individual batch need not increase monotonically even after the policy has discovered high-quality regions of the operator space. The cumulative best curve provides complementary view of learning: once high-quality solution is discovered, it remains part of solution archive even while subsequent trajectories explore alternative regions. The late-time fluctuations should therefore not be interpreted as loss of previously learned solutions, but rather as consequence of continued exploration in qualitydiversity search. Figure 1: Learning curve of the RL policy for seed=42. For each training batch, the mean χ2 relative to the SM is shown, together with the maximum χ2 discovered up to that batch. The mean and maximum curves are smoothed using 10-batch rolling average; the faint light green curve shows the corresponding unsmoothed values.

sections.title: 5 Exploration of the SMEFT Operator Space
sections.content: In this section, we analyze the viable SMEFT solutions5 discovered by the RL agent. To identify these solutions, post-training, we collect all candidate solutions sampled by the policy during training and rank them according to their χ2 values w.r.t. the SM. 5We use the terms solutions, hypotheses, theories or operator sets interchangeably throughout the text. 9 We stress that, policy optimized solely for fit quality can repeatedly return to the neighborhood of previously discovered high-quality operator set, generating many solutions that differ by only one or few operators. Such solutions can be distinct as exact operator sets while representing essentially the same underlying neighborhood in operator space. Our objective is instead to discover both high-quality solutions and broad range of structurally distinct operator combinations. The diversity term in Eq. (18) addresses this issue by rewarding solutions that have small Jaccard overlap with the existing archive of high-quality theories. To quantify the resulting coverage of SMEFT hypotheses, we distinguish between exact solutions corresponding to unique operator sets, and solution families which group sufficiently similar operator sets according to their Jaccard similarity. Exact solutions: Each candidate theory is specified by its set of active operators S. For illustration, we consider theory solution if it satisfies χ2 > 100 relative to the SM, and we count two solutions as the same exact solution if they contain identical operator sets, irrespective of operator order. Solution families: To quantify how many structurally different solutions are found, we additionally group exact solutions into families using the Jaccard similarity. Solutions are processed in the order in which they are discovered, batch by batch. new solution is compared with the stored family representatives {Rk}. If J(S, Rk) > 0.5 for any k, is assigned to an existing family and the number of families is unchanged. Otherwise becomes the founder of new family and is stored as its representative. Thus the founder of family is the first solution encountered that is not similar to any earlier representative, and is not necessarily the solution with the largest χ2. Because membership is defined only relative to the representative, it is not transitive, and the precise family count depends mildly on the discovery order. The same procedure and threshold are applied to the RL archive and to both random baselines as discussed below. 5.1 Comparison with random-search baselines Figure 2: Cumulative number of high-quality SMEFT solutions discovered during the training as function of batch. Only theories with χ2 > 100 relative to the SM are retained. Exact operator sets and Jaccard families are shown for the RL agent and the random-search baselines. The randomsequential baseline follows the same step-wise construction and acceptance procedure as the RL agent but proposes operators uniformly at random. To benchmark the RL search, we consider two random-search baselines with comparable computational budgets. In the random-subset baseline, the number of operators in each subset is chosen randomly, and the corresponding operators are then sampled independently from the full operator space and evaluated directly. This provides simple measure of how frequently high-quality hypotheses can be found through unguided sampling of the combinatorial operator space. The second benchmark, the random-sequential baseline, follows the same sequential construction and acceptance rule as the RL agent, but selects each proposed operator uniformly at random. This provides more direct algorithmic comparison because both methods construct theories sequentially and receive the same physics evaluation, but only the RL agent uses learned state-dependent policy to select the next operator. Fig. 2 compares the cumulative discovery of solutions satisfying χ2 > 100 during the RL training. This threshold deliberately focuses the comparison on high-quality theories rather than on the total number of sampled configurations. The exact-solution count measures the number of unique operator sets discovered, whereas the family count provides more stringent measure of operator diversity defined by 0.5. The comparison therefore probes two complementary aspects of the search: (i) whether the learned policy can concentrate on SMEFT operator space containing good fits and (ii) whether it can continue to discover distinct regions rather than repeatedly sampling small variations of the same operator set, e.g. by changing one SMEFT operator. These results show that the RL search fulfills our objective of not only maximizing χ2 but also efficiently exploring the high-quality regions of the SMEFT operator space. 5.2 Coverage across independent training seeds Because RL training is stochastic, independent runs can converge toward different regions of the SMEFT operator space. However, this feature can be exploited by combining the solution archives obtained from multiple training seeds. Fig. 3 shows the cumulative coverage obtained by combining Figure 3: Cumulative coverage of the SMEFT solution space obtained by combining independent RL training runs. Only theories satisfying χ2 > 100 are included. The curves show the cumulative numbers of distinct exact operator sets and Jaccard families as additional training seeds are included. ten independently trained RL policies. Exact operator sets typically grow more rapidly than the number of families because different runs can discover variations of the same underlying structures. The family curve therefore provides the more informative measure of whether additional independent training runs continue to probe genuinely different regions of operator space. In this figure, the continued growth of the family count indicates that additional runs still uncover new structures, whereas saturation would suggest that the dominant families accessible to the search have largely been identified. sections.title: 6 Conclusions and Future Prospects
sections.content: In order to interpret complex patterns of anomalies with respect to the SM, we have formulated an RL method that can be used to search for viable SMEFT operator hypotheses sequentially. This 12 addresses the central challenge of the combinatorial explosion of possible hypotheses within SMEFT. Our formulation provides novel approach to this problem by learning an actorcritic RL policy. Importantly, our objective differs from naive optimization problem in an important respect. We are not interested only in the SMEFT hypothesis that maximizes the improvement in χ2. Because several structurally different SMEFT scenarios may provide good descriptions of the same data, mapping this degeneracy is crucial for NP model building in bottom-up approach. We therefore introduced diversity reward based on Jaccard similarity, turning the search into qualitydiversity problem in which the RL policy is rewarded both for improving the global fit and for exploring operator sets different from those already discovered. We tested the framework in challenging environment containing 132 observables from several sectors, including 24 hypothetical measurements with discrepancies larger than 1.5σ relative to the SM predictions. The RL agent searched over 912 candidate SMEFT operators and constructed hypotheses sequentially while accounting for the effects of each operator proposal on all observables. The resulting learning behaviour shows that the policy is able to identify 26 high-quality solutions with Jaccard indices below 0.1. Our comparisons with random-subset and random-sequential search baselines provide direct benchmark of both search efficiency and solution diversity, while independent training seeds offer systematic way of extending the coverage of the operator space. Several extensions are natural. The present framework can be applied to larger observable sets and updated experimental measurements, and the qualitydiversity objective can be refined to target specific requirements of the physics problem. It will also be useful to investigate how policies trained on one pattern of experimental discrepancies transfer to modified datasets, and whether the learned search strategy can be amortized across related SMEFT inference problems. More broadly, the approach developed here illustrates how RL can complement conventional phenomenological reasoning by systematically exploring theory spaces whose combinatorial complexity makes exhaustive human-guided analysis increasingly difficult. To facilitate the broader application of our framework, we also provide an open-source Python package, ReinforceSMEFT, that can be readily installed via pip, enabling users to train and apply the RL agent to their own phenomenological analyses.
